title: The kiss and the linen (Mark 14:43–52)
hook: betrayed with a kiss; a young man flees naked, a detail only Mark keeps

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Abba, the family word for father, prayed face down in Gethsemane. Did you say plainly what you wanted, and let it go? Day two hundred twenty-two.

He's still speaking to his sleepy friends when the torches appear through the olive trees. Judas, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. In the dark, they need to be sure they grab the right man, so Judas has given them a signal. In the King James Bible: "Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead him away safely." A kiss of greeting was likely how a student greeted a teacher, as ordinary as a handshake. So Judas walks straight up to Jesus, says, "Master, master," and kisses him. Mark uses a stronger word for the kiss here, and many readers hear it as warm, the way you'd greet someone you love.
screen: `TORCHES THROUGH THE OLIVE TREES.` → `THE SIGNAL IS A KISS.` → `MASTER, MASTER.`

segments.voice: They seize him. Someone standing by pulls a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. Mark doesn't say who; John's Gospel later names Peter. Jesus speaks to the crowd: have you come out with swords and clubs as if I were a bandit? Day after day I was with you in the temple, teaching, and you didn't arrest me. But let the scriptures be fulfilled. And then the sentence the whole evening has been leading to: "And they all forsook him, and fled." All of them. A few hours ago they all said they'd die with him. Now every one of them is running through the dark. Then Mark tells us something so strange that Matthew and Luke leave it out entirely. "And there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body." They grab him, and he wriggles out of the cloth and runs off naked, leaving them holding the linen. Who was he? The text is silent. An old guess says it was Mark himself, signing his gospel with an embarrassing memory. Some readers hear an echo of the prophet Amos: on that day even the bravest will flee away naked. Others notice the linen, because a linen cloth will appear again later in this story, and so will a young man. What's clear is the picture. One last follower, trying to stay close, and when they grab him, he leaves everything and runs. Christians have often seen themselves in these verses. Not in the kiss, but in the running. And they notice that the one who was left alone is the one who does not run.
screen: `A SWORD, AND AN EAR.` · `THEY ALL FORSOOK HIM, AND FLED.` · `A YOUNG MAN IN A LINEN CLOTH.` · `WHO WAS HE? THE TEXT IS SILENT.` · then, large: `AND THEY ALL FORSOOK HIM, AND FLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you run. Settle, and breathe. Everyone has a way of fleeing when things get hard. Some people go silent. Some go busy. Some scroll. Some make a joke. Some leave the room. What's yours? Don't scold yourself; just notice it, the way you'd notice a habit in a friend. Picture the last time you ran, and what you left behind in the soldiers' hands. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God honestly. The bell holds the time.
The kiss and the linen. A friend's greeting used as a signal, and a young man who fled, leaving his linen cloth behind.
screen: `THE KISS AND THE LINEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: they all fled. Today, when you feel the urge to run from something hard, notice it, and stay one minute longer. Day two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Christians remember the arrest on Maundy Thursday night and Good Friday, and many churches strip the altar bare in silence after the Thursday service as a sign of Jesus left alone.

fork.setup: you're one of the twelve. torches, swords, a kiss, and your teacher is seized. hours ago you swore you'd die with him. what do you do?
fork.reveal: "they all forsook him, and fled." every one. the last to follow was a young man who ran off, leaving his linen behind.

original.note: Greek: fine linen cloth. the young man's covering in Mark 14:51.

trapdoor: what you thought: Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss, and that's the story.
what it means: a greeting of love used as a signal, and then every friend runs, down to the last young man.
what a scholar hears: kataphileō, often read as a warm kiss; the young man found only in Mark, perhaps Mark himself, perhaps an echo of Amos 2:16.

sources.quoted: Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead him away safely.

notes: The kiss as a customary greeting of a disciple to a teacher: common commentary claim; confirm.

kataphileō as an intensive, warm kiss is debated (in Koine it can simply mean 'kiss'); hook softened from 'The Greek word means he kissed him warmly' to 'many readers hear it as warm'. Kiss-of-greeting custom softened to 'likely'. Confirm.
'The soldiers grab him' changed to 'They grab him': Mark 14:51 says 'the young men laid hold on him', not soldiers.
The young man as Mark himself is an old but unproven guess; Amos 2:16 echo is a scholarly suggestion. Both stated as guesses.
Forward hints: the teach says a linen cloth and a young man appear again later (15:46, 16:5) without naming the scenes. Confirm this light foreshadowing is wanted.
howItsDone: stripping of the altar on Maundy Thursday is Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran practice, not universal; 'many churches'. Confirm.
